{{Short description|Fractal curve}}
The '''Fibonacci word fractal''' is a [[fractal curve]] defined on the plane from the [[Fibonacci word]].

== Definition ==
[[File:Fibonacci fractal first iterations.png|thumb|The first iterations]]
[[File:Fibonacci curve L-system.png|thumb|L-system representation<ref>Ramírez, José L.; Rubiano, Gustavo N. (2014). "[https://www.mathematica-journal.com/2014/02/properties-and-generalizations-of-the-fibonacci-word-fractal/ Properties and Generalizations of the Fibonacci Word Fractal]", ''The Mathematical Journal'', Vol. 16.</ref>]]

This curve is built iteratively by applying the Odd–Even Drawing rule to the [[Fibonacci word]] 0100101001001...:

For each digit at position ''k'':
# If the digit is 0:
#* Draw a line segment then turn 90° to the left if ''k'' is [[parity (mathematics)|even]]
#* Draw a line segment then turn 90° to the right if ''k'' is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]]
# If the digit is 1:
#* Draw a line segment and stay straight
To a Fibonacci word of length <math>F_n</math> (the ''n''<sup>th</sup> [[Fibonacci number]]) is associated a curve <math>\mathcal{F}_n</math> made of <math>F_n</math> segments. The curve displays three different aspects whether ''n'' is in the form 3''k'', 3''k''&nbsp;+&thinsp;1, or 3''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2.

== Properties ==
[[File:FWF whites quares.png|thumb|The Fibonacci numbers in the Fibonacci word fractal.]]
Some of the Fibonacci word fractal's properties include:<ref>Monnerot-Dumaine, Alexis (February 2009). "[http://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00367972/fr/ The Fibonacci word fractal]", independent (''hal.archives-ouvertes.fr'').</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=1601.04786|title=Hausdorff Dimension of Generalized Fibonacci Word Fractals|last1=Hoffman|first1=Tyler|last2=Steinhurst|first2=Benjamin|class=math.MG|year=2016}}</ref>
* The curve <math>\mathcal{F_n}</math> contains <math>F_n</math> segments, <math>F_{n-1}</math> right angles and <math>F_{n-2}</math> flat angles.
* The curve never self-intersects and does not contain double points. At the limit, it contains an infinity of points asymptotically close.
* The curve presents self-similarities at all scales. The reduction ratio is <math>1+\sqrt{2}</math>. This number, also called the [[silver ratio]], is present in a great number of properties listed below.
* The number of self-similarities at level ''n'' is a [[Fibonacci number]] \&nbsp;−1. (more precisely: <math>F_{3n+3}-1</math>).
* The curve encloses an infinity of square structures of decreasing sizes in a ratio <math>1+\sqrt{2}</math> (see figure). The number of those square structures is a Fibonacci number.
* The curve <math>\mathcal{F}_n</math>can also be constructed in different ways (see gallery below):
** [[Iterated function system]]  of 4 and 1 homothety of ratio <math>1/(1+\sqrt2)</math> and <math>1/(1+\sqrt2)^2</math>
** By joining the curves <math>\mathcal{F}_{n-1}</math> and <math>\mathcal{F}_{n-2}</math>
** [[L-system|Lindenmayer system]] 
** By an iterated construction of 8 square patterns around each square pattern.
** By an iterated construction of [[octagon]]s 
* The [[Hausdorff dimension]] of the Fibonacci word fractal is <math>3\,\frac{\log\varphi}{\log(1+\sqrt 2)}\approx 1.6379</math>, with <math>\varphi = \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}</math> the [[golden ratio]].
* Generalizing to an angle <math>\alpha</math> between 0 and <math>\pi/2</math>, its Hausdorff dimension is <math>3\,\frac{\log\varphi}{\log(1+a+\sqrt{(1+a)^2+1})}</math>, with <math>a=\cos\alpha</math>.
* The Hausdorff dimension of its frontier is <math>\frac{\log 3}{{\log(1+\sqrt 2})}\approx 1.2465</math>.
* Exchanging the roles of "0" and "1" in the Fibonacci word, or in the drawing rule yields a similar curve, but oriented 45°.
* From the Fibonacci word, one can define the «dense Fibonacci word», on an alphabet of 3 letters: 102210221102110211022102211021102110221022102211021... {{OEIS|id=A143667}}. The usage, on this word, of a more simple drawing rule, defines an infinite set of variants of the curve, among which:
** a "diagonal variant"
** a "svastika variant"
** a "compact variant"
* It is [[conjecture]]d that the Fibonacci word fractal appears for every [[sturmian word]] for which the slope, written in [[Continued fraction|continued fraction expansion]], ends with an infinite sequence of&nbsp;"1"s.

== The Fibonacci tile ==
[[File:Tiling Fibonacci word fractal.png|thumb|Imperfect tiling by the Fibonacci tile. The area of the central square tends to zero.]]
The juxtaposition of four <math>F_{3k}</math> curves allows the construction of a closed curve enclosing a surface whose [[area]] is not null. This curve is called a "Fibonacci tile".
* The Fibonacci tile almost tiles the plane. The juxtaposition of 4 tiles (see illustration) leaves at the center a free square whose area tends to zero as ''k'' tends to infinity. At the limit, the infinite Fibonacci tile tiles the plane.
* If the tile is enclosed in a square of side 1, then its area tends to <math>2-\sqrt{2} = 0.5857</math>.
[[File:Tiling by Fibonacci tiles.jpg|thumb|Perfect tiling by the Fibonacci snowflake]]

=== Fibonacci snowflake ===
<!--"Fibonacci snowflake" redirects directly to this section.-->
[[File:Fibonacci snowflakes 2 1, 2, 3, and 4.svg|300px|thumb|Fibonacci snowflakes for ''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 for ''n''&nbsp;=&thinsp;1 through 4: <math>\sideset{}{_1^\left [ 2 \right ] \quad}\prod</math>, <math>\sideset{}{_2^\left [ 2 \right ] \quad}\prod</math>, <math>\sideset{}{_3^\left [ 2 \right ] \quad}\prod</math>, <math>\sideset{}{_4^\left [ 2 \right ] \quad}\prod</math><ref>Ramírez, Rubiano, and De Castro (2014). "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397514000851 A generalization of the Fibonacci word fractal and the Fibonacci snowflake]", ''Theoretical Computer Science'', Vol. 528, p.40-56. [https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.1368]</ref>]]

The '''Fibonacci snowflake''' is a Fibonacci tile defined by:<ref name="Blondin">Blondin-Massé, Alexandre; Brlek, Srečko; Garon, Ariane; and Labbé, Sébastien (2009). "[https://doi.org/10.1007%2F978-3-642-04397-0_7 Christoffel and Fibonacci tiles]", ''Lecture Notes in Computer Science: Discrete Geometry for Computer Imagery'', p.67-8. Springer. {{ISBN|9783642043963}}.</ref>
* <math>q_n = q_{n-1}q_{n-2}</math> if <math>n \equiv 2 \pmod 3</math>
* <math>q_n = q_{n-1}\overline{q}_{n-2}</math> otherwise.
with <math>q_0=\epsilon</math> and <math>q_1=R</math>, <math>L =</math> "turn left" and <math>R =</math> "turn right", and <math>\overline{R} = L</math>.

Several remarkable properties:<ref name="Blondin" /><ref name="Blondin2">A. Blondin-Massé, S. Labbé, S. Brlek, M. Mendès-France (2011). "[http://www.slabbe.org/Publications/2011-fibo-snowflakes.pdf Fibonacci snowflakes]".</ref>
* It is the Fibonacci tile associated to the "diagonal variant" previously defined.
* It tiles the plane at any order.
* It tiles the plane by translation in two different ways. 
* its [[perimeter]] at order ''n'' equals <math>4F(3n+1)</math>, where <math>F(n)</math> is the ''n''<sup>th</sup> [[Fibonacci number]]. 
* its area at order ''n'' follows the successive indexes of odd row of the [[Pell number|Pell sequence]] (defined by <math>P(n)=2P(n-1)+P(n-2)</math>).
